paragraphs: Aldus Manutius ran his press in Venice with a scholar's aims rather than a merchant's: he wanted accurate texts of the Greek and Latin classics available to readers who could not afford, or find room for, the huge folio volumes universities used. In 1501 his type designer Francesco Griffo cut a new slanted typeface modelled on humanist cursive handwriting, which let more text fit on a page without losing legibility.

Manutius paired the new type with his other project, the octavo-format libri portatiles, pocket-sized books meant to be carried and read outside a library. The combination made cheap classical texts portable for the first time. The slanted style, called italic after its Venetian origin, was quickly copied across Europe and now marks emphasis and titles rather than whole pages of text.

Indian mathematicians had worked out a positional decimal system, where a digit's value depends on where it sits in a number and a zero holds an empty place, well before it reached the Islamic world. The system let arithmetic be done directly on the written numerals themselves, rather than requiring an abacus or counting board, a real practical advance over the Roman numerals still used across much of Europe.

Arab scholars, notably al-Khwarizmi, adopted and described the system in works later translated into Latin, and it was through those translations that Europe came to know the digits as Arabic numerals, obscuring their Indian origin. The word algorithm even derives from al-Khwarizmi's own name, reflecting how his description of the system shaped later mathematics.

The Achaemenid Persian Empire stretched from Egypt to the edge of India, ruling peoples who spoke dozens of languages and used almost as many scripts. Rather than impose Persian, the administration adopted Aramaic, already established as a trade language across the Near East, as the written medium for royal correspondence and provincial bookkeeping.

Officials in Egypt, Babylon and Bactria who shared no spoken language could read the same Aramaic memo, which is largely why the empire could run as a single bureaucracy at all. The habit outlasted the empire itself: Aramaic remained the working language of the region long after Persian rule ended, and its alphabet went on to shape the scripts later used for Hebrew and Arabic.

Before 405, Armenian had no dedicated script of its own, and Armenian Christians read scripture in Greek or Syriac, languages most of the congregation could not follow. The monk Mesrop Mashtots, working with a Greek calligrapher named Rufinus, designed a set of thirty-six letters, matched closely enough to Armenian's actual sounds that it could represent the spoken language precisely rather than approximate it through a borrowed script.

The alphabet's first major work was a translation of the Bible, followed by a wave of original theological and historical writing in Armenian, later called the golden age of Armenian literature. Two more letters were added centuries later for foreign sounds, but the core of Mashtots's system has stayed in continuous use for over sixteen centuries.

By the early 1960s, every computer manufacturer had its own scheme for representing letters as binary numbers, so a file written on one machine often came out as garbage on another's. The American Standards Association's committee, with input from IBM's Bob Bemer, settled a common seven-bit code in 1963, assigning fixed values to English letters, digits, punctuation and control characters for teletypes and printers.

Because ASCII covered only the basic Latin alphabet, it left out accented letters and every non-Latin script, a limitation that became obvious as computing spread beyond English-speaking countries. It became the common ground letting American computers, terminals and early networks exchange plain text reliably, and its first 128 code points still sit unchanged at the base of Unicode.

Darius I had the text carved high on a limestone cliff in western Iran, in three cuneiform scripts, Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian, describing his rise to power and his suppression of rebellions after the death of Cambyses II. The location was deliberately inaccessible, cut into rock above a spring on the old road between Babylon and the Persian heartland, so it could be seen but not easily reached or damaged.

That same inaccessibility is what preserved it long enough to matter. In the 1830s British officer Henry Rawlinson had himself lowered on ropes to copy the inscription, and because the Old Persian text could be worked out first, it was the key to cracking the other two scripts. Comparing all three let scholars finally read Babylonian and Assyrian cuneiform at scale.

Brahmi first appears clearly in the edicts of the emperor Ashoka, carved onto pillars and rock faces across the Indian subcontinent to publicise his Buddhist policies to subjects who spoke many different languages. The script organised sounds by how they are produced in the mouth, grouping consonants by place of articulation in a way that later scripts across Asia inherited wholesale.

As Buddhism and trade carried the script outward, local scribes reshaped its letterforms to fit Tibetan, Burmese, Thai, Khmer and Javanese, among many others, so that today's radically different-looking Asian scripts often share the same underlying logic. A reader trained in one Brahmi-derived script can often work out the basic structure of another purely from the shared arrangement of vowels and consonants.

Before this reform, manuscripts across Europe were copied in a tangle of regional hands, some barely legible outside their own monastery. Charlemagne's court, seeking uniform texts across a sprawling empire, backed scribes, notably at the monastery of Corbie, in developing a clear, rounded lowercase script with consistent spacing and separated words.

The new hand spread through monastic scriptoria copying classical Latin as much as religious texts. This had an unplanned side effect: when Renaissance scholars sought ancient Roman texts, most of what survived had been copied in Carolingian minuscule, and they mistook it for ancient writing. Early printers modelled their typefaces on it, which is why lowercase letters today still resemble a script devised for Charlemagne's monks.

Claude Chappe demonstrated his design to France's revolutionary government in 1792: a wooden mast topped by a movable crossbar with a jointed arm at each end, whose positions an operator in a distant tower could read through a telescope and copy onto the next tower in the chain. The arms could form 196 combinations, each standing for a word, letter or phrase from a codebook.

The Convention funded a line of these towers from Paris to Lille, and on 15 August 1794 the network carried its first message, reporting that a besieged garrison had surrendered, far faster than any rider could manage. The network expanded to cover much of France under Napoleon and stayed in government use for decades, until the electric telegraph made relay towers obsolete.

Sequoyah could not read English and had never been formally schooled in any writing system when he began working out a way to write Cherokee around 1809. After experimenting with pictographs and abandoning them as unworkable, he settled on assigning a symbol to each syllable of the spoken language rather than each sound, borrowing shapes from Latin, Greek and Hebrew letters he had seen.

He finished the eighty-six-character system in 1821 and taught it first to his young daughter, Ahyokah, then demonstrated it to Cherokee leaders by having her read back messages she had never heard spoken. Because each symbol maps directly onto a familiar sound, the system could be learned in days rather than years, and most of the Cherokee Nation was reported literate in it within about five years.

Zhou dynasty workshops cast ritual vessels, cauldrons, wine vessels, basins, with inscriptions built directly into the mould, not added afterward. Some record only a clan's name, but others run to several hundred characters, describing a king's grant of land, a military campaign or the reason the vessel was commissioned in the first place.

Because bronze survives burial far better than the bamboo strips and silk that Zhou scribes also wrote on, these vessels preserve some of the fullest surviving Chinese texts from the period. Scholars still use bronze inscriptions to check and correct later historical accounts, since a vessel cast to commemorate an event is a far more direct witness than a history written centuries afterward.

Before anyone in Mesopotamia wrote a word, they counted with clay. Small moulded shapes, cones, spheres, discs, stood in for specific goods: a particular token for a jar of oil, another for a sheep. Archaeologist Denise Schmandt-Besserat catalogued thousands of these tokens from sites across the region and argued they were the ancestor of writing itself, not merely a bookkeeping curiosity.

The system's own success strained it. Traders began sealing tokens inside hollow clay envelopes to prevent tampering, then pressed the tokens into the envelope's wet surface, leaving a record on the outside matching what was sealed within. That outer impression was the useful part. Once scribes realised they could skip the tokens and just mark the clay, the envelope's picture became a sign, and counting began sliding toward script.

A scroll had to be unrolled with both hands and read in strict sequence, which made finding a specific passage slow and awkward. The codex, sheets folded and stitched at one edge much like a modern book, let a reader flip directly to any page, write on both sides of the material, and fit far more text into a single portable object.

Early Christian communities adopted the codex especially fast, likely because it suited cross-referencing scripture during worship far better than unrolling a scroll to the right point each time. Pagan Roman literature stuck with scrolls for longer out of tradition, but by the fourth century the codex had become the standard format across the Mediterranean world, and it never really lost that position afterward.

Richard Outcault's cartoon Hogan's Alley began running in Joseph Pulitzer's New York World in February 1895, depicting a chaotic tenement alley full of ragged children. One boy in an oversized nightshirt, bald and jug-eared, became the strip's breakout figure; readers and rival papers started calling him simply the Yellow Kid once his nightshirt was printed in a new yellow ink in January 1896.

The strip is credited with popularising the speech balloon as a regular device, letting characters talk directly on the page instead of a caption underneath. Its commercial success, and the bidding war it triggered when William Randolph Hearst poached both the character and Outcault to a rival paper, helped fix the newspaper comic strip as a recurring weekly feature rather than a one-off novelty.

Woodblock illustrations, the usual way to illustrate printed text, could only hold lines as fine as a knife could cut into a plank without the wood splitting. Engravers scratched their designs into a sheet of copper instead, using a burin to cut grooves far finer than any woodcut, then forced ink into those grooves and wiped the surface clean before pressing damp paper onto the plate.

The technique let mapmakers and illustrators render coastlines, hachured hills and tiny place names at a level of detail impossible before, which is why atlases from the later sixteenth century onward look sharper than their woodcut predecessors. The cost was speed: an engraved copper plate wore down after a few thousand impressions and needed re-cutting, while relief woodblocks lasted far longer and stayed cheaper for books.

A cylinder seal is a small stone drum, often no bigger than a finger, carved in reverse with figures or inscriptions and rolled across wet clay to leave a continuous strip of impression. Rolling rather than stamping let a single small object cover a large document, and the design could not be easily copied without the physical seal itself.

Officials and merchants wore theirs on a cord or pin so they were always within reach, using them to close storage jars, authenticate contracts and mark who had approved a shipment. Because the carved scenes changed with fashion and status, ranging from banquet scenes to mythological combat, surviving seals now let archaeologists date layers of a site almost as precisely as an inscription would.

A colophon at the end of the scroll records that it was made on 11 May 868, on behalf of a man named Wang Jie, for free distribution in honour of his parents, giving it a documented date centuries earlier than any comparably certain printed book from Europe. Seven printed sheets of paper were glued together into a scroll roughly five metres long, with a woodcut illustration of the Buddha preaching at the front.

It survived because it was sealed, with tens of thousands of other manuscripts, inside a hidden chamber at the Mogao caves near Dunhuang, likely for safekeeping, and was not found until the early twentieth century. The care taken over its wording and the maturity of the woodblock technique show printing had already developed in China well before this copy survived with its date intact.

Latin and Greek had been written without spaces for over a thousand years. Ancient readers were trained to read aloud, sounding out where one word ended and the next began as they went, which made the unbroken run of letters, called scriptio continua, workable for a practised scribe even though it looks impossible today. Irish monks, copying Latin as a foreign language rather than a mother tongue, had no such training to lean on.

Working in scriptoria from around the seventh century, they began inserting gaps between words to make text parseable at a glance rather than by ear. The change spread through monastic copying networks across the British Isles and onto the continent over the following centuries, making silent, rapid reading possible for the first time.

The earliest hieroglyphs were not decoration on a temple wall but labels tied to jars. Small bone and ivory tags found at Abydos, marked with signs for places and quantities, are among the oldest known examples, used to track goods delivered to an early ruler's tomb rather than to record a sentence.

Full hieroglyphic writing grew out of that administrative need, combining pictures that stood for whole words with others that spelled out sounds, so a single sign might mean a thing or just a syllable depending on context. Priests kept the system alive for temple inscriptions for over three thousand years after everyday Egyptians had moved to faster cursive scripts.

Machines that could scan and transmit an image over a telephone line had existed in incompatible forms since well before 1980, but a fax bought from one manufacturer could not talk to one from another, which kept the technology a niche tool for a few large organisations. The International Telecommunication Union's Group 3 standard, finalised in 1980, fixed a common scanning resolution and compression method any compliant machine could use.

That single standard let a fax machine bought in Tokyo exchange a legible page with one bought in London without either side worrying about compatibility. Prices fell as manufacturers built to the same specification, and office fax machines went from a rarity to a near-universal fixture within a decade, carrying contracts and signatures years before email could send an image.

Elizabeth Mallet, a printer who had spent years in the less respectable trade of publishing the confessions of condemned prisoners before their execution at Tyburn, launched the Daily Courant from her premises near Fleet Bridge on 11 March 1702. It was a single sheet, printed on one side only, carrying translated digests of foreign news with the other side left for advertisements.

Mallet deliberately avoided reporting on English domestic politics, since anything she got wrong or that officials disliked could be traced straight back to a named publisher operating openly. She sold the paper on after running it for only about forty days, but the format she had started, one page, printed every day rather than weekly, continued under new owners for roughly three decades and set the template daily papers still follow.

Shigetaka Kurita designed his set of pictographs in 1999 for NTT DoCoMo's i-mode mobile internet service, working within a strict twelve-by-twelve pixel grid because that was all the phone screens of the day could display. His 176 symbols drew on manga conventions, weather icons and existing text emoticons, covering everyday needs like a phone, a heart, rain clouds and a handful of facial expressions.

DoCoMo was not first with the idea itself; a rival carrier, SoftBank, had shipped a smaller set of ninety pictograms two years earlier. Kurita's set became more influential because DoCoMo's dominant market share carried it into wide use, and its symbols fed into the emoji later adopted into the Unicode standard.

Paper had reached Europe through Muslim Spain centuries earlier, but Fabriano, a small town in central Italy, was where an industrial-scale mill took hold in 1276, run on the town's clean mountain streams. Fabriano's papermakers made two changes that mattered more than the mill itself: they sized sheets with animal gelatine instead of starch, making the paper far more durable, and pressed a wire design into the pulp to leave a watermark.

Both innovations spread across Europe and stayed in use for centuries; the watermark became the standard way papermakers signed and dated their work. Rag paper from mills like Fabriano's was cheaper to produce in quantity than parchment made from animal skin, and that price gap, more than any single invention, is what let books multiply in the two centuries before printing arrived.

Paper had been made in China for centuries before the knowledge travelled west, and one persistent account credits its spread to Chinese papermakers captured after the Battle of Talas in 751, who ended up passing the craft on in Samarkand. Whether or not that story is precisely accurate, the technique took hold quickly across Central Asia and reached Baghdad within a generation.

Paper was cheaper to produce than parchment and far more practical than papyrus once removed from Egypt's dry climate, and Baghdad under the Abbasid caliphs put it to immediate use. The city's paper mills fed a booming book trade and supported institutions like the House of Wisdom, where scholars translated and copied Greek, Persian and Indian texts at a scale that would have been unaffordable on parchment alone.

Music before 1501 was printed, when at all, in two separate passes: staff lines run through the press once, then notes stamped or drawn on afterward by hand, a slow method prone to misalignment. Ottaviano Petrucci, working in Venice, solved this by casting movable type for noteheads and combining it with a second pass of staff lines, aligned enough that a printed page of polyphonic music could be read as reliably as a manuscript.

His first publication, the Harmonice Musices Odhecaton, printed in 1501, collected nearly a hundred secular songs by composers working across France, Italy and the Low Countries. Petrucci held an exclusive Venetian printing privilege and issued further volumes of masses and motets over the following two decades, though the slow triple-impression process kept printed music rare and costly.

Handwritten newsletters circulating among merchants and courts had carried foreign news for decades before 1605, but they were copied one at a time and reached only whoever could pay a scribe. Johann Carolus, a bookseller and printer in Strasbourg, took the next step by setting that same kind of digest in movable type and issuing it on a fixed weekly schedule.

Printing let a single edition reach far more readers at little extra cost, and the fixed schedule meant readers knew when to expect the next one, features that separated a newspaper from an occasional pamphlet. Carolus later said he had assembled the same digests by hand for years and switched to print simply to save the copying, an origin more mundane than the format it produced.

A silcrete flake found at Blombos Cave carries a cross-hatched grid drawn with an ochre crayon rather than incised with a tool. Researchers dated the layer to roughly 73,000 years ago using thermoluminescence on nearby burnt stone, pushing the earliest known deliberate drawing back by tens of thousands of years from what had previously been assumed.

The same cave has produced engraved ochre blocks, perforated shell beads and shell containers apparently used to mix pigment, all from people using the Still Bay stone tool tradition. None of it proves what the pattern meant to the person who drew it, but the repetition of the same grid motif across several pieces suggests it was a shared convention, not a doodle made once and forgotten.

Most typists in the 1880s still hunted for each key with their eyes on the keyboard, the same way most people type with one or two fingers today. Frank McGurrin, a court reporter from Michigan, had taught himself to strike every key from memory using all ten fingers without looking down, an approach nobody else was known to use in competition at the time.

On 25 July 1888 in Cincinnati, McGurrin faced Louis Traub, who typed with eight fingers but watched his hands, in a public contest covered by newspapers nationwide. McGurrin won decisively and collected a $500 prize, and touch typing began to be taught deliberately rather than picked up by accident. Whether he invented the method or simply demonstrated it best is still debated.

A large deposit of pure graphite was found near Borrowdale in Cumberland in the mid sixteenth century, and locals at first mistook the soft black mineral for a form of lead, hence the term still used for pencil cores today. Graphite marks paper cleanly and, unlike actual lead, is not toxic, but raw lumps of it are brittle and smear the hand holding them.

Encasing sawn sticks of Borrowdale graphite in wood solved that problem and gave writers, mapmakers and artists a tool that could be sharpened, erased with a rubbed crumb of bread, and carried without staining a pocket. Borrowdale graphite was unusually pure and needed no binder, which is why England held a near-monopoly on decent pencils for over two centuries, until continental makers learned to fire powdered graphite with clay.

Phoenician writing worked well for Phoenician, a Semitic language where consonants carry most of the meaning and vowels can often be inferred. Greek needed them spelled out, so when Greek speakers adopted the Phoenician letters they repurposed a handful of consonant signs that Greek did not need for its own sounds, turning them into the first dedicated vowel letters, alpha, epsilon, iota and others.

That adaptation produced a script where every sound, vowel included, got its own symbol, a genuinely new kind of precision rather than a borrowed convenience. Because the direction it was written still wandered for a while, sometimes right to left, sometimes alternating line by line, the fully settled left-to-right Greek alphabet familiar today took another century or so to stabilise fully.

For generations before any of it was written, singers performed the Iliad and Odyssey from memory, using formulaic phrases and fixed metrical patterns as scaffolding that let a performance run for hours without a script. The poems as we have them are the product of that oral tradition being caught in writing once the Greek alphabet made recording long verse practical.

Exactly when that first happened is not something a single date can pin down. What is clearer is the consequence: fixing the wording in writing let the epics travel and be copied consistently across the Greek world, rather than drifting performance by performance the way oral poetry naturally does. Later Athenian editors, including under the tyrant Peisistratos, are credited with standardising the text further still.

The script shows up on thousands of small stone seals, pottery shards and copper tablets across cities like Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, usually in short strings of five signs or fewer. No inscription longer than about seventeen signs has ever turned up, which is part of why nobody has managed to read it: there simply is not enough continuous text to test a theory against.

Over a hundred attempts at decipherment have been published, proposing links to Dravidian, Sanskrit and other language families, and none has won broad acceptance. Some researchers have even argued the marks are not language at all but symbols of ownership or ritual meaning, closer to a set of trademarks than a sentence. Without a bilingual find like the Rosetta Stone, the debate has nowhere to be settled.

Classical Chinese had no way to render Japanese grammar: its particles, verb endings and honorifics did not exist in the borrowed script. Scribes began using a handful of Chinese characters purely for their sound, stripped of meaning, to spell those endings out phonetically. Over the ninth century that shorthand simplified into two syllabaries, hiragana and katakana, each built from a few dozen strokes.

Hiragana in particular became associated with women, who were largely barred from the Chinese-based education given to court men. That association turned into an advantage: writers working in kana produced diaries, poetry and romances in a vernacular formal Chinese prose could not match. The Tale of Genji and the Pillow Book, both written by court women, show what the new syllabaries made possible.

Samuel Johnson had promised his publishers a three-year project when he signed the contract in 1746; the work took closer to nine, much of it carried out with a small team of copyists in a house on Gough Square in London, sorting quotations from centuries of English literature onto slips of paper. He defined around 40,000 words and illustrated many with quoted examples of use, a scale no earlier English dictionary had attempted.

Johnson's definitions were not always neutral. His entry for lexicographer, as a harmless drudge who busies himself in tracing the etymology of words, is often quoted, and his political opinions occasionally crept into supposedly straightforward definitions. The dictionary remained the standard reference for English for roughly a century, until the Oxford English Dictionary began to replace it.

Early Rome sat within reach of Etruscan cities that had already adapted the Greek alphabet for their own language, and Latin speakers borrowed that Etruscan version rather than going to Greek directly. Several letters had to be reshaped or dropped because Etruscan and Latin used different sounds, which is why the Latin alphabet ended up neither a copy of Greek nor of Etruscan but its own working compromise.

Rome's later expansion did the rest. As the empire's administration, army and church spread the script across Western Europe, it displaced most of the region's older local writing systems, from runes to Iberian scripts, and outlasted the empire itself. It remains the most widely used alphabet on earth, adapted with added letters and diacritics for languages Rome never encountered.

Linear B tablets were never meant to last. Palace scribes at Knossos and Pylos used them as one-year administrative records, tracking rations, textiles and land grants, and expected to recycle the clay afterwards. The tablets that survive only did so because fires that destroyed the palaces baked them hard, preserving accidentally what was designed to be temporary.

Michael Ventris, an architect working outside academia, cracked the script in 1952 by testing the hunch that it wrote an early form of Greek centuries before Homer, a possibility most classicists had dismissed. His decipherment pushed the attested history of the Greek language back roughly seven hundred years and confirmed that Mycenaean palace culture, long known only through Homeric legend, kept detailed written accounts of its own economy.

Before Ottmar Mergenthaler's machine, setting a page of type still meant a compositor picking individual metal letters out of a case by hand, one at a time, exactly as it had since Gutenberg. Mergenthaler, a German-born clockmaker working in Baltimore, built a keyboard-driven machine that assembled brass letter moulds into a line, cast the whole line as a single slug of hot metal, and then melted the moulds down to be reused for the next one.

Thomas Edison reportedly called it the eighth wonder of the world when he saw it demonstrated. The New York Tribune installed the first production Linotype in 1886, and the machine spread through the newspaper industry because a single operator could now set type roughly as fast as several compositors working by hand.

Alois Senefelder was a Bavarian playwright trying to find a cheap way to print his own scripts when he noticed, by accident, that a greasy crayon mark he had made on a slab of limestone resisted water. He worked out that if he wetted the stone and rolled ink across it, the ink stuck only to the greasy drawing, letting him pull a print from a flat surface with no cutting or etching at all.

That was the break from every earlier printing method, which depended on carving relief or engraving grooves into wood or metal. A lithographic stone could reproduce a pencil or crayon drawing's exact texture, which made the process valuable for sheet music, maps and illustration where fine tonal shading mattered. Senefelder patented the process in 1799, and it dominated image printing into the twentieth century.

The project that became the Oxford English Dictionary was proposed to the Philological Society in 1857, an attempt to record every English word and every shift in its meaning, backed by dated quotations showing each usage in context. Its first editor, James Murray, worked out of a corrugated iron shed in his garden that he called the Scriptorium, sorting millions of quotation slips sent in by volunteer readers.

Murray died in 1915, before the work was finished, and the complete first edition, ten volumes covering roughly 400,000 words, was not published until 1928, seventy-one years after the project began. Unlike Johnson's dictionary, which relied on one man's reading, the OED's method of dated citations drawn from a volunteer network became the model most later historical dictionaries followed.

Panini's Ashtadhyayi, the Eight Chapters, compresses Sanskrit grammar into roughly four thousand terse rules, arranged so that later rules override earlier ones according to strict precedence, closer to a formal algorithm than to a descriptive grammar book. A student had to hold much of the system in memory to apply it correctly, since the rules were built to be combined rather than read in isolation.

Twentieth-century linguists and computer scientists noticed the resemblance to a programming language before Sanskrit grammarians had ever imagined such a thing existed, and some early work on formal grammar theory drew directly on Panini's method. The text still underlies how classical Sanskrit is taught, not as a historical curiosity but as the working reference grammar many traditional scholars use.

A story told by the Roman writer Pliny credits Pergamum's development of parchment to a rivalry: Egypt allegedly cut off papyrus exports to stop the city's library from rivalling Alexandria's, forcing Pergamene craftsmen to perfect treated animal skin as a substitute. Historians treat that account with some suspicion, since skins had long been used for writing, but Pergamum's name stuck to the material.

Whatever its origin, parchment offered real advantages papyrus could not match outside Egypt's climate: it did not need a reed that grew only along the Nile, it could be scraped clean and reused, and it held up far better to folding rather than rolling. That durability under folding is precisely what let books written as codices, rather than scrolls, become practical in the following centuries.

Adobe co-founder John Warnock circulated an internal memo in 1991 under the codename Camelot, describing a file format that would let a document look identical on any screen or printer. The team built it by stripping Adobe's PostScript printing language to its descriptive core and adding a way to embed the actual fonts used, so a page would not substitute a different typeface.

Adobe released the format as PDF on 15 June 1993, alongside three companion programs bundled as Acrobat: Distiller to create PDFs, Exchange to edit them, and a free Reader so anyone could open one without buying Adobe software. The free reader mattered more than the format's technical elegance, since a PDF someone sent could always be opened, and it became the default way to exchange documents that had to look the same everywhere.

Italian archaeologist Luigi Pernier found the disc on 3 July 1908 in an underground deposit at the Minoan palace of Phaistos, on Crete's southern coast. Both faces carry a spiral of stamped symbols, 241 signs made from just 45 distinct stamps pressed into the clay before it was fired, a method that has never turned up on any other object from the Bronze Age Aegean.

That is precisely what makes it so hard to explain. A found object with no companion pieces gives scholars nothing to cross-check a reading against, so proposed translations, some treating it as a hymn, others as a game board or calendar, have never converged on agreement. Its authenticity was even questioned for decades, though it is now generally accepted as genuine and sits on display in Heraklion.

Sei Shonagon was a lady-in-waiting to Empress Teishi at the Heian court, and around the year 1000 she began keeping a private notebook of observations, lists and complaints entirely in kana. Formal writing at court still meant Chinese characters, a script reserved largely for men, so writing in the vernacular was not a stylistic flourish but a way around an education she had been denied.

The result reads less like a diary than a collection of opinions: things that are elegant, things that are annoying, things glimpsed once and never forgotten. Its miscellany form, jumping between anecdote and list without narrative order, had no real precedent in Chinese or Japanese writing. Alongside Murasaki Shikibu's contemporary Tale of Genji, it is treated as one of the two founding works of classical Japanese prose.

Inscriptions found at turquoise mines in the Sinai Peninsula show Semitic labourers borrowing Egyptian hieroglyphic signs but using them for a completely different purpose. Instead of the complex mix of sound and meaning hieroglyphs relied on, each sign was assigned one consonant, based on the Semitic word for the object it represented, so a picture of a house, bet, stood simply for the sound b.

That single change, one sign per sound, is what made the system learnable in days rather than years of scribal training. It spread among traders and labourers who had no access to formal Egyptian education, and its descendants eventually branched into Phoenician, then Greek, then Latin, meaning the letters on this page trace back to workers scratching marks near a mine.

The Sholes and Glidden typewriter, built by Christopher Latham Sholes and sold from 1873 through the gunmaker E. Remington and Sons, was not the first typewriter, but the first sold widely enough to fix a keyboard layout in the public's hands. Sholes rearranged his early alphabetical layout repeatedly, and the popular claim that he did it to slow typists down and stop the mechanical type-bars jamming is disputed.

What is certain is that the arrangement stuck once the machine sold and touch typists trained on it in large numbers, making any later, more efficient layout a hard sell against millions of already-trained fingers. The layout has outlived the mechanical type-bar it was supposedly built around.

Julius Caesar, as consul, ordered official proceedings of the Senate and public notices posted where citizens could read them, a practice that continued and expanded under later emperors into the Acta Diurna, boards displayed in the Forum listing trial outcomes, births into prominent families, military reports and public announcements.

Nothing about it resembled a printed newspaper. There was no press run, no distribution beyond the Forum itself, and copies existed only because individual readers or their slaves transcribed the boards by hand for correspondents living elsewhere in the empire. It was a single public notice board rather than a publication, but it filled the role a newspaper would later fill: telling a city what its government had just done.

Roman cursive was never meant to be admired. Where the formal capital letters carved on monuments were slow and deliberate, everyday cursive joined strokes together and simplified letterforms so a scribe writing a letter, a receipt or a legal document could move the pen quickly across wax or papyrus without lifting it constantly.

The script looks almost unrecognisable next to the monumental capitals most people picture as Roman writing: formal inscriptions were built for permanence and display, cursive for speed and volume. Surviving examples, including letters unearthed at the fort of Vindolanda near Hadrian's Wall, show soldiers writing about supplies, socks and dinner invitations in a hand that later evolved into medieval European scripts.

Fewer than thirty wooden rongorongo tablets survive, most removed from Easter Island by missionaries and collectors in the nineteenth century. The glyphs run boustrophedon: each line reads in the opposite direction to the one before it, and every other line must be rotated a half-turn to be read, which has made even a tablet's correct orientation a matter of dispute.

No bilingual text or other decoding key has surfaced. By the time outsiders asked islanders what the glyphs said, the few who could read them were already dead or knew only fragments. Proposed dates range from long before European contact to influence from watching the Spanish sign an 1770 document; no reading is accepted as reliable.

Every printing press before Richard Hoe's, however fast, still worked on the same basic principle as Gutenberg's: a flat bed of type pressed once against a flat sheet, one impression at a time. Hoe's innovation was to curve the type itself, locking individually cast pieces onto the surface of a rotating cylinder, so paper could be fed continuously past it instead of being pressed and lifted with each sheet.

The 1843 machine could print several times faster than flatbed presses, and later versions with multiple cylinders pushed the rate further still. Newspapers once capped by how many copies a single press could pull in a night could now print large runs before dawn, a shift behind the rise of mass-circulation dailies on both sides of the Atlantic.

Alexandria's large Jewish community increasingly spoke Greek rather than Hebrew, and a translation project, according to tradition undertaken by seventy or seventy-two scholars, rendered the Torah and later the rest of the Hebrew scriptures into Greek. The name Septuagint, from the Latin for seventy, comes directly from that legendary number of translators.

Whatever the truth behind the number, the translation had consequences well beyond Alexandria's synagogues. Early Christian writers, most of whom read Greek rather than Hebrew, quoted scripture from the Septuagint rather than the Hebrew original, and it became the version of the Old Testament that shaped how the New Testament writers themselves referenced earlier scripture.

Timothy Bright was a physician, not a stenographer by trade, and his 1588 book Characterie was pitched at English readers as a way to write speech down as fast as it was spoken. Rather than abbreviating letters, his system assigned roughly five hundred separate symbols to whole words, built from eighteen basic geometric shapes with twelve further marks that could be added to each one to shift its meaning.

Elizabeth I granted Bright an exclusive fifteen-year privilege to print books of this kind, treating the method as valuable enough to protect. Learning five hundred arbitrary symbols by heart made the system demanding compared with later letter-based shorthands, and only a handful of copies survive today, several incomplete. It is generally credited as the first published shorthand system in English.

Carnegie Mellon's computer science bulletin board ran on plain text with no way to signal tone, and a physics joke about mercury spilling in a fake elevator-safety warning had already been misread as a real hazard alert. Scott Fahlman posted a message at 11:44 a.m. on 19 September 1982 suggesting people use the character sequence colon, hyphen, close-parenthesis to mark a joke, and its reverse for anything meant seriously.

The message survived by accident: Fahlman's own university erased its early bulletin board archives, and the original post was only recovered years later from a backup tape kept at another institution. His sideways face is now generally credited as the first emoticon proposed for digital text, a small fix for a problem, misread sarcasm, that has never really gone away online.

Ugarit's scribes took the wedge-shaped strokes of cuneiform, a script built for hundreds of syllable signs, and stripped it down to roughly thirty marks, each standing for a single consonant sound. The result looked like Babylonian cuneiform on the clay tablet but worked like an alphabet, letting a trained scribe learn the whole system in a fraction of the time.

Tablets recovered from the ruined city cover myths, letters, legal contracts and even a list of the alphabet's signs in order, essentially an ancient primer. That ordering closely resembles the sequence still used in Hebrew and Arabic today, which is part of why Ugaritic is treated as an early branch in the alphabet's family tree rather than an isolated local experiment.

ASCII's seven-bit code left room for only 128 characters, enough for English but nowhere near enough for Chinese, Arabic, Cyrillic or the dozens of other scripts computers needed to display. Incompatible regional encodings filled the gap, so the same byte could mean a different letter depending on whose software wrote it. Unicode 1.0 arrived in 1991, assigning a single fixed number to every character across every script it covered.

Early Unicode allotted sixteen bits per character, room for roughly 65,000 symbols, which strained further once later versions added historical scripts, technical symbols and emoji. Software took the rest of the 1990s to be rewritten to support it, but Unicode is now the encoding behind almost every website, phone and document exchanged across language boundaries.

A wax tablet was a shallow wooden frame filled with a thin layer of blackened beeswax, written on with a pointed stylus and erased by smoothing the wax flat with the stylus's blunt end. Schoolchildren practised letters on them, merchants drafted contracts before copying a final version onto papyrus, and travellers folded several tablets together, hinged like a small book, to carry notes and letters.

Because the wax could be melted and reset endlessly, tablets were the era's genuinely disposable writing surface, meant for drafts, homework and short-lived messages rather than anything meant to last. Surviving examples, including hinged sets recovered from Roman forts in Britain, show ordinary daily writing, requisitions, personal letters, birthday invitations, that papyrus and stone rarely bothered to preserve.
